response.translation: [226] But [he says] that in growing bodies the heat is not much in respect of substance, at least given the small bulk of their body, nor in respect of the increase of the quality, for it does not appear hotter than that of those in their prime. In the strength of its proper works, then, he concedes that the heat of growing bodies excels, but [holds] that it is not said in the proper sense. Now his passage, in which he will make these points clear, is very long. But I think I shall do now just as I did with the passage written out earlier. For that one too, being very long, I did not write out whole, but selected only its most pertinent part. Let it be done in the same way, then, with this one too, and let the part of it most useful for the matter in hand be written out. The one of my two arguments, then, has now reached its end, and I would come to the remaining one; for you will surely remember that I set out two inquiries right at the beginning: one, whether Hippocrates rightly added 'innate', the other, whether he rightly said that heat is greatest in growing bodies.

The other inquiry, then, having been [227] completed, I would now turn to this remaining one and attempt to examine whether it has been rightly said that heat is greatest in growing bodies. Now in examining one heat against another, there happen to be three things that require inquiry, and these very far separated from one another: one, what it is for one heat to be more than another; another, what it is for one thing to be hotter than another; and the third, what it is for one heat to be stronger than another. If, then, someone should happen to ask us of what sort is the heat that is more than another, we ought to answer analogously to what we would answer to another who asked of what sort is one moist thing that is more than another. For just as here, the question being directed in the first place to what was said, it is no longer correct to answer anything else than only this, that what exceeds in substance is more: one would, of course, say that the amphora [holds] more liquid than the half.
uncertain_greek: πρῶτον τὸ ἐπερώτημα πρὸς τὸ εἰρημένον

response.translation: So too in the case of heat: if someone were to put this same question, of what sort is the heat that is more than another, we would not rightly [228] answer anything other than that which is more in substance, because, plainly, it has more substance and extends over a larger place. And nothing will prevent the same thing from being both more heat and hot to a lesser degree, just as the liquid that is more in substance could be fluid to a lesser degree. To this question, then, one would answer correctly in this way; but to that other one, of what sort is one thing hotter than another, the correct answer is: that which is more intensified in warmth, even if it happens to be in a smaller substance. Just as, to one asking of what sort is one thing whiter than another, the correct answer is: that which is more intensified in the white quality. In this respect at any rate, even if snow happens to be in a small bulk, one would say that it is whiter than any other white thing whatsoever; just as also, to one asking of what sort is one thing moister than another, the correct answer is: that which is more fluid, as water [is moister] than honey and pitch, even if the water is observed in a very small substance, and the honey and the pitch in excess.

So also, [229] to one asking about heat of what sort is one thing hotter than another, it is correct to answer: that which is most intensified in warmth, as fire, even though it is observed in a small substance, [is hotter than] some other hot and lukewarm thing that is compared with it and happens to exist in a larger substance. To these questions, then, these are the answers; but to one who inquires of what sort is one heat stronger than another, the answer is no longer like the previous ones. For we shall answer neither that which is more intensified in warmth nor that which is observed in a larger substance, but that which excels in the accomplishment of the work. What I am saying would be established thus: the works of heat are, I suppose, many. For some things are melted by it, and others it solidifies, and it changes a great many things; and, to speak in detail, in our bodies it concocts the nutriment in the stomach and the intestines, and brings the worked-up [nutriment] up into the body, and alters it into body and makes it grow onto our bodies, namely in nutrition and growth.

The stronger heat, then, is that which will be able to provide [230] these things more. And what happens to be such is not in every case that which is either intensified in quality or more in substance. For often what is less in substance and less in warmth is most effective for the work. For, as we said before, for the performance of the proper works it is not what is most intensified that is stronger, but what is most well-proportioned. For what is intensified in warmth itself sometimes even becomes a harm to the works; and sufficient and most credible proofs of this, to my mind, are the things I went through earlier when speaking about the distinctive property of heat.
uncertain_greek: τὸ δὲ τυγχάνον ὂν οὐχὶ πάντως

response.translation: This being so, and the things inquired into in comparing one heat with another being three, as I said before, when Hippocrates says here that growing things have the most innate heat, [he does] one of three things: either, using this word in its proper sense, he has said something false; or he has used the word badly and said something false; or else, in order that he may seem to have said something true, [231] it must be that he has not used the word well. For if he says that the heat is most in growing bodies, for instance in respect of substance, as one might say that the liquid of the amphora is most, not that of the double of it, he will seem to have used the word correctly, but he must necessarily have said something very false. For the heat in growing bodies is not most in substance, since the bulk of the body is not greater in them than in those in their prime and the old. And the innate heat is extended throughout the whole body.
uncertain_greek: τοῦ ἀμφορέως, οὐ τὸ διπλάσιον τούτου

response.translation: If, on the other hand, he says that it is more in growing bodies and that this warmth is intensified, perhaps [meaning] hotter than that, as one might speak who wished to say that snow is whiter than some other white thing, [meaning] not that it is whiter or more white, but that its white is more than this white, then Hippocrates will seem to err in both respects, both in not using the word well and in saying something false besides. He would seem to err in not using the [232] word well, because he placed this word, which is applied to more substance, wishing to signify that a quality more intensified in warmth is present. And he would seem to have said something false, because the heat in growing bodies is not most intensified in quality, not as it should be, hotter in this age than in any other. But he said that it is most intensified in growing bodies; and that this is false, that heat is most intensified in growing bodies, it is easy for anyone to recognise. For no sign would be found present in the body of growing persons of a greatest intensification of heat in warmth. For what was said by him in the treatise On the Nature of Man, as evidence that heat is most in growing bodies, is altogether foolish. For [he says] that he declares man to be hotter in the first period of life, inferring this from the growth that is then accomplished in the greatest measure.

'For the nutriment would not,' he says, 'be carried upward by force and contrary to nature, in the direction opposite to its own [233] weight, in the growing of the body, unless what compels it were something strong.' For of such a thing the sign is not that the heat is more intensified in warmth, but that it is stronger. And the stronger, as I said a little before, was not such as that which is most intensified in its quality, but that which is most well-proportioned to the work. Since, then, these things are so, if Hippocrates says thus, 'growing things have the most innate heat', he errs in both respects, both in not using the word well and in saying something false besides. But if he says it in the third way I mentioned, that heat is most in growing bodies in the sense of the strongest for the accomplishment of the work, which comes from being most well-proportioned, and not from either being more in substance or being most intensified in warmth itself, then he would seem to have used the word well, in that he said the heat is 'most' when he ought to have said 'strongest'; yet what was said would seem to have been rightly stated.
uncertain_greek: τὸν μάλιστα ἐπιτεταμένον κατὰ αὐτοῦ ποιότητα

response.translation: For since growth comes about through the [234] innate heat, as the argument will show, it is impracticable and impossible that it should not be strongest in growing bodies. And in this connection what is in the treatise On the Nature of Man would, to my mind, have been well said: 'For it is necessary that the body, as it grows and advances by force, should have its heat strongest.' Such too is the passage of Lycus, extended in length, but expressing nothing more than what I said before. For if Hippocrates, measuring by the bulk of the substance, said that the heat is more in growing bodies, he [Lycus] thinks that he errs, since the body of children is clearly smaller. And if [he meant] what is intensified in warmth, again he says that the phenomenon conflicts with this too. But if [he meant] what is stronger in activity, he concedes that something true is being said, but declares that he has not used the expression well. For [he says] the heat of growing bodies ought to have been called not 'more', but 'stronger' with respect to activity.

[235] But, my excellent Lycus, someone, I think, might say to him, speaking in defence on the points on which he abuses Hippocrates, these statements are not bad. To begin with, the heat that is more in substance is not judged simply by the bulk of the whole body, but in the way that Lycus himself said elsewhere that man has the largest brain, not taking the size simply, but according to the proportion of animal to animal. Just as, then, he says that so small a child has a larger brain than the largest elephant, not directing his attention to the bulk of the body alone, but adding to it the consideration according to proportion, so also in the case of the hot body he ought to have done, considering what sort of body among those within us is innate, that is, primordial. For he himself knows the name both as written in the Hippocratic books and as joined to that body which is present from the beginning in those that are generated, that is, the body from which they have had their first genesis.
